newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 13.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--Government and teachers are unmoved from their respective corners of the ring, with students trapped in the middle. Prime Minister Costas Simitis and Education Minister Gerasimos Arsenis told representatives of high school teachers at their meeting last night that there were no margins for more wage demands: at a resulting meeting, teachers voted to extend their strike for a fifth week.

--The Cyprus problem is a danger to stability in the wider region, US Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who said she hoped the island-republic's entry to the European Union could provide an opportunity for progress. Asked if pressure could be exerted on Ankara, she said that Turkey was of major importance to the US.

--Following the refusal recently of a priest to conduct rites for the funeral of a woman married in a civil ceremony, the government said yesterday it could examine the possibility of 'civil, non-religious' funeral rites.

--Striking teachers will rally in downtown Athens today following their decision to continue their strike. "We will continue until we are vindicated," they said in response to Simitis's refusal to consider their demands any longer.

--Dimitra Liani-Papandreou, the widow of late ruling party PASOK president and founder Andreas Papandreou, made one of her rare public appearances last night to attend the unveiling of a series of stamps on Papandreou, letting loose a few volleys at 'grey' politicians who do not respect Papandreou's work.

--The tax department is to conduct snap checks on VAT payments on 3,500 firms to collect 100 billion drachmas by June, rather than waiting for regular checks which can take up to seven years to collect dues.
--Simitis closed the door on a compromise with teachers last night, saying there could be talks on institutional demands but not economic.

--Investigations continuing into the murder of a Russian underworld figure have revealed he lived a life of wine, women and song in Greece, residing in luxury seaside homes costing 20 million drachmas per year.
--Good returns for those with the confidence to invest in the Athens stock exchange: 50 shares have seen a dizzying increase in value since the beginning of the year.

--An enthusiastic reception last night for the opening of the National Gallery's latest exhibition "The Greek Revolution, Delacroix and the French artists". The thousands of Greeks who responded to the invitation to the official inauguration were unable to get into the exhibition and forced to queue outside.
--Dialogue on the fate of the social security system begins tomorrow with increasing retirement age to 66-67 one of the issues.

--There is still no sign of the young woman kidnapped at gunpoint from her father's home in Crete by her estranged husband. Constantine Canarakis, 28, and his two accomplices are being sought by police, who say, however, that the case is "a family matter".
--Cervical cancer is caused by a virus and can be transmitted by sexual contact, Greek researchers at Thessaloniki University claimed yesterday. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
